detailed_rationale:
Quality Power Electrical Equipments (QPOWER) manufactures high-voltage electrical equipment for grid connectivity and energy transition -- power generation, transmission, distribution and automation -- serving global clients in critical energy-transition infrastructure, including sophisticated niches like FACTS (Flexible AC Transmission Systems). Recent order wins illustrate both the domestic and export dimensions of the business: a Rs 15.70 crore domestic order for 400 KV instrument transformers (July 2026) and a Rs 40.9 crore FACTS supply order in Japan, executable by December 2027 (July 2026) -- the Japan win in particular signals genuine technological credibility in a demanding, quality-sensitive export market.

FY26 (year to March 2026) revenue was Rs 222 crore with net profit of Rs 55 crore; TTM net profit growth is a very strong 81% (compounded), with Q4 FY26 alone contributing Rs 71 crore sales / Rs 16 crore profit. The balance sheet is almost debt-free with solid ROCE (~19.9%). A genuine working-capital-quality concern surfaced in the sources reviewed: debtor days rose from 82 to 102, and overall working-capital days rose to 119 -- cash conversion is deteriorating even as reported growth remains strong, a real signal worth tracking rather than a stale-data artifact. The stock trades at a very rich valuation (PE cited as high as ~163x in the most current source, versus ~76x on the quant sheet's own reference point, implying continued substantial re-rating since the quant snapshot was taken).
recommendation_rationale: Quant already rates this Hold on both horizons (final scores 84.8/71.0); the underlying energy-transition/grid-equipment demand backdrop and export order wins (Japan FACTS order) are genuinely constructive, but the combination of an extremely rich and apparently still-rising valuation multiple with deteriorating working-capital metrics (rising debtor/WC days) argues for caution rather than a rescue upgrade -- both risks and opportunities are real here, and Hold appropriately reflects that balance.
summary: Quality Power Electrical Equipments makes specialized high-voltage electrical gear for power grids and the energy transition, and has recently won a notable export order in Japan alongside solid domestic order flow. Growth and returns have been strong, but the stock is priced very richly, and its collection of receivables (how quickly it gets paid) has been slowing even as revenue grows -- worth watching closely. We rate it a Hold: a genuine niche energy-transition player, but priced for perfection with an emerging cash-conversion flag.
positive_para: Winning a FACTS supply order in Japan is a meaningful technological and credibility signal in a demanding export market, on top of steady domestic high-voltage equipment orders, and the balance sheet is almost debt-free with solid returns on capital (~20% ROCE) -- a genuinely well-capitalized niche player riding a real, multi-year global grid-modernization and energy-transition capex cycle.
negative_para: Debtor days rising from 82 to 102 and overall working-capital days reaching 119 is a genuine cash-conversion deterioration, not noise, and needs to be watched closely, particularly for a company this small in absolute revenue terms (~Rs 222 crore FY26). At a trailing PE reported as high as ~163x, the stock is priced for years of continued hypergrowth with no room for a stumble, and even modest order lumpiness (given the company's small absolute order sizes, Rs 15-40 crore each) could disappoint a market pricing in much more.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At a trailing PE in the 75-165x range (quant sheet vs. more current sources) against ROCE of ~20%, the market is pricing many years of sustained hypergrowth in a still-small-revenue-base business (~Rs 222 crore FY26) -- a very high bar, made higher by the emerging working-capital deterioration. The energy-transition/grid-equipment tailwind is real and durable, but this specific valuation assumes near-flawless execution for an extended period. Call: rich, priced for perfection; a name to watch rather than one offering a margin of safety.
